Abstract.AbstractText: The outer membrane (OM) of Gram-negative bacteria is a complex and asymmetric bilayer that antimicrobial peptides must disrupt in order to provoke the cell lysis. The inner and external leaflets of the OM are mainly composed of phospholipids (PL), and lipopolysaccharide (LPS), respectively. Supported lipid bilayers are interesting model systems to mimic the lipid asymmetric scaffold of the OM and determine the quantitative and mechanistic effect of antimicrobial agents, using complementary physicochemical techniques. We report the formation of asymmetric PL/LPS bilayers using the Langmuir-Blodgett/Langmuir-Schaefer technique on two different surfaces (sapphire and mica) with synthetic phospholipids constituting the inner leaflet and bacteria-extracted mutant LPS making up the outer one. The combination of neutron reflectometry and atomic force microscopy techniques allowed the examination of the asymmetric scaffold structure along the normal to the interface and its surface morphology in buffer conditions. Our results allow discrimination of two structurally related peptides, one neutral and inactive, and the other cationic and active. The active cationic plasticin PTCDA1-KF disrupts the asymmetric OM at relevant concentrations through a carpeting scenario characterized by a dramatic removal of lipid molecules from the surface.
